Following Apple's announcement of changes to the European version of the App Tracking Transparency feature, the company is now rolling out a simplified App Store commission structure for developers in Europe. Here are the details.

Apple overhauls business terms for EU app developers

Apple had previously announced eight changes to the European version of its App Tracking Transparency feature in response to an investigation by German antitrust regulators.

Apple now says the new commission structure will take effect in Europe on October 1, including reducing the external purchase commission to 15% and replacing the controversial "Core Technology Fee" with a 5% "Core Technology Commission."

The move comes more than a year after Apple announced major changes to its EU App Store, which introduced a range of complicated rules. You can read about that here.

Below is Apple's statement:

Apple also announced new terms for App Store commission rates, alternative app payment options, and the distribution of apps through alternative app marketplaces or websites.

The new terms are as follows:

For App Store apps using Apple's in-app purchase system, the commission will be 26%. The vast majority of developers—including those participating in the App Store Small Business Program, Mini Apps Partner Program, or Video Partner Program, as well as subscribers who auto-renew after the first year—will pay a 15% commission. For App Store apps using alternative payment options, the commission will be 20%. Developers in the above programs will pay a lower commission of 10%. For App Store apps that direct users to a website to complete a transaction, the commission will be 15%. Developers in the above programs will pay a lower rate of 10%. For apps distributed through an alternative app marketplace or website, Apple will charge a 5% Core Technology Commission.

Under the new terms, provided developers meet Apple's "presentation requirements" and keep their chosen payment method for 12 months, they may offer both Apple's in-app purchase and alternative payment options within their app or via a link out to a website.

Today's announcement from Apple also includes new child safety protections and alternative payment arrangements for the EU, which include:

Apps in the App Store's Kids category may not include links that direct users to a website to complete a transaction, to reduce the risk of fraud or deception targeting children. For users under 18, all App Store apps that use alternative payment options or direct users to a website to complete a transaction must include parental supervision features that require younger users to involve a parent or guardian before making a purchase. For users under 13, apps on the App Store may not link out to a website to complete a transaction, to prevent the risk of fraud targeting young children.

Apple added that in EU member states where children over 13 are required to have parental consent to engage in digital activities, "these protections will be adjusted accordingly."

Finally, Apple's latest announced changes also expand the eligibility criteria for operating an alternative app marketplace or distributing apps through a website.

The expanded eligibility criteria include:

Achieving a moderate financial stability threshold in its Dun & Bradstreet rating. Being a publicly traded company or owned by one. Having received funding from a recognized investment institution's venture capital fund. Having a financial audit completed by a licensed accountant. Being a government agency, educational institution, or non-profit organization.

Apple noted that the website distribution option currently available only in the EU lacks the ongoing oversight of a marketplace operator, which could allow bad actors to "operate for extended periods before being discovered, harming users."

Therefore, Apple said it will continue to require all apps distributed through alternative channels to go through its Notarization process.

To learn more about today's announcements, visit this link.

Update: A European Commission spokesperson responded to Bloomberg's statement, welcoming Apple's adjustments and noting that the changes were the result of "close dialogue" with the company. The spokesperson added that the Commission will monitor Apple's implementation of the new terms.
